results.content: # *Edmond de Belamy*. ***Edmond de Belamy***, sometimes referred to as ***Portrait of Edmond de Belamy***, is a generative adversarial network (GAN) portrait painting constructed by Paris-based arts collective **Obvious** in 2018 from WikiArt's artwork database. It gained media attention after Christie's announced its intention to auction the piece as the first artwork created using artificial intelligence to be featured in the "Prints & Multiples" sale at the Christie's Images New York auction. Seven minutes into the bidding, an anonymous phone bidder won the auction with a US$432,500 bid, and the print was bought for US$432,500 on 25 October 2018, making it the second most expensive artwork in the auction, just cheaper than Andy Warhol's artwork, *Myths "Myths (Warhol)")*, the 254 cm × 254 cm 1981 artwork that was sold for US$780,500. *Edmond de Belamy* is the fictional descendant of *Madame de Belamy*, a name that was given to another artificial intelligence (AI) artwork made by Obvious.

By clicking Continue to join or sign in, you agree to LinkedIn’s User Agreement, Privacy Policy, and Cookie Policy. # The Auction of "Edmond de Belamy": AI Enters the Art World. In October 2018, the prestigious auction house Christie's made headlines when it auctioned off a portrait titled "Portrait of Edmond de Belamy." What set this artwork apart from others was not the subject matter or the style, but rather the fact that it was created by an artificial intelligence using a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN). The GAN, a type of machine learning model, generated the portrait of "Edmond de Belamy" based on its analysis of the input data. Both art fans and collectors were drawn to "Edmond de Belamy" despite its unusual beginnings. Christie's chose to include the piece in one of their auctions after realizing its significance as a trailblazing example of artificial intelligence-generated art. Below, Pierre Fautrel, the Obvious co-founder, is seen standing next to "Edmond de Belamy" prior to its auction at Christie's in New York. The exorbitant cost sparked concerns about the value of AI-generated art and its place in the creative process, in addition to highlighting the growing demand for this kind of art. The auction of "Edmond de Belamy" spurred discussions about authorship and creativity in the era of artificial intelligence within the art community. Even though an artificial intelligence produced the artwork, humans eventually had a hand in it since Obvious's creators were instrumental in both training the GAN and selecting the best pieces. This made it harder to distinguish between human and machine creativity, which sparked debates over what constitutes art and the place of artists in the digital era. In conclusion, the Christie's auction of "Edmond de Belamy" represented a critical turning point in the fusion of artificial intelligence and art.

The Wayback Machine - https://web.archive.org/web/20181107115532/https://observer.com/2018/10/ai-created-portrait-of-edmond-belamy-christies-worth-it/. *The Portrait of Edmond Belamy*, a painting of a blurry, portly gentleman that was generated via algorithm by an artificially intelligent system, has just sold at Christie’s Auction House for $432,500, far surpassing its high estimate of $10,000. The creation of the painting was supervised by the Paris-based art collective Obvious, who are humans, but the painting itself was produced entirely by a “generative adversarial network,” an AI program that uses machine learning to survey and subsequently generate original imagery. According to BBC, “The AI system compares its own portraits against ones made by humans and keeps working on them until it is unable to tell the difference between the two.” In other words, the impetus behind the creation of *Edmond Belamy* was to create an image of a face that doesn’t actually exist, but is rather an approximation or an aggregate of hundreds of thousands of actual human faces. Selling an AI-generated work at auction seems like mostly a cheap gimmick to make art sales relevant and interesting to the vast majority who have no need or ability to attend one. The sale had the added bonus of enticing novelty-loving, non-art-world-types with cash to burn. To the credit of the French collective Obvious (could that name be any better), it totally worked. ***Subscribe to Observer’s Arts Newsletter***. Hugo Caselles-Dupré, Pierre Fautrel and Gauthier Vernier of the Obvious collective are, to be frank, exactly what their name suggests. “Men are blinded by fame, power and money,” reads the caption on another one of their AI-generated paintings.
